newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Tale of two cities in capital stakes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Tale of two cities in capital stakes.

text.p: Pretoria is in her purple prime, jacaranda blossoms ablaze against azure skies. Cape Town is emerging from the rainy season, bursting with brilliant greens and the promise of another glorious, wine-laden summer.
Between them, the battle lines are drawn for a showdown over which city will end up as the permanent legislative capital of post-apartheid South Africa.

Under a compromise dating back to before the First World War, glamorous Cape Town, a beautiful city on a dramatic peninsula between the Indian and Atlantic oceans, has long been the seat of parliament. It does not want to lose this honour.

Worthy Pretoria, a dour, inland metropolis of red brick and glass towers, is home to the administrative and executive arm of government. Pretorians feel that logic dictates a unification of legislature and executive, under one metropolitan roof.

In the past, key legislators with wives, children, servants, would conduct a stately shuttle between the two cities, travelling the 1,500 Km (950 miles) from Pretoria to the Cape in January and returning in June.
Even diplomatic missions followed the seasonal migration, as the core of South Africa's government switched location.
But the political pace was slower then. The country was clamped under all-white rule, the numbers in parliament were less than half today's and the sessions were shorter.

In the 1990s, the two-capital tradition is becoming a luxury and a major inconvenience. Ministers are torn between staying close to their civil servants in Pretoria and close to the decision-making -- and voting -- process in Cape Town.
Telephone links can accomplish only so much. For key meetings, a hurried shuttle flight may be the only solution.
So pressure mounts to find a single home.

But as Germany found with its planned move of the Bundestag from Bonn to Berlin, a city gets attached to having a parliament, an entrenched civil service does not move easily, and the two may be difficult to reconcile.
South Africa's most famous son, President Nelson Mandela, is remaining above the fray, and has admonished other party leaders for taking sides. Still, he presses for a "considered" choice.
"But I am saying I want a decision soon. We can't afford to continue this two capital thing - it's too expensive. One way or the other, we must decide," Mandela told Reuters recently.

Cape Town has the handsome old parliament buildings redolent of South Africa's colonial past. But Pretoria hosts 32 hefty state departments and 102 diplomatic missions -- an accumulation of institutions far too massive to contemplate moving.
So the choice, effectively, comes down to uniting government under Pretoria's flag or maintaining the status quo with changes to cut costs and boost efficiency.

F.W. de Klerk's white-led National Party and the small Democratic Party have thrown their weight behind declaring Cape Town the capital. But Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) is hopelessly divided, avoiding what could be a bruising internal wrangle by declining to force a decision.
"The cities are making the running," said Speaker of Parliament Frene Ginwala.

The two cities' rivarly is as old as the 1910 treaty that welded Britain's Cape and Natal colonies, the Orange Free State and President Paul Kruger's Transvaal Republic into the Union of South Africa under British rule.
Pretoria was declared administrative capital, Cape Town was made seat of parliament and the Orange Free State was given the Appeal Court.

Under white rule, 178 legislators migrated from Pretoria to the Cape every January for a ceremonial opening of parliament with horse parades and gun salutes and diplomats, journalists and senior officials in tow. In June, they packed up, despatched the servants and headed back to Pretoria.
But since the advent of democracy, the parliamentary year has stretched to eight months and Cape Town's small airport is daily abuzz with the back and forth of 490 elected MPs.
Research commissioned by the Pretoria Capital Initiative, a broadly-based association of interested parties, put the cost of all this at $18 million a year at least.
"We cannot afford luxuries like that," commented PCI spokesman and Pretoria businessman Andy Shoredits. "We need every penny we have. No country in the world has two capitals."
Cape Town's Citizen's Alliance for Parliament rejects Pretoria's arithmetic and argues it would cost the country $48 million a year to move the legislature from Cape Town.
Alan Dunn, editor of Pretoria News and former correspondent in Cape Town, wants Parliament in Pretoria.

"Cape Town people are really poets and wine drinkers," he sniffs. "While they have the beaches and the mountain, nothing else apart from tradition speaks in favour of having the national legislature in South Africa's farthest corner."
